the credit provider believes on reasonable grounds that the individual has committed a serious credit infringement;
the provider uses the information in connection with the infringement; or
the use is required or authorised by or under an Australian law (other than the consumer data rules) or a court/tribunal order; or
the use is a use prescribed by the regulations.
Permitted disclosures
Subsection (1) does not apply to the disclosure of credit eligibility information about the individual if:
the disclosure is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual; or
the disclosure is to a related body corporate of the credit provider; or
the disclosure is to:
a person for the purpose of processing an application for credit made to the credit provider; or
a person who manages credit provided by the credit provider for use in managing that credit; or
both of the following apply:
the credit provider believes on reasonable grounds that the individual has committed a serious credit infringement;
the provider discloses the information to another credit provider that has an Australian link, or to an enforcement body; or
both of the following apply:
the disclosure is for the purposes of a recognised external dispute resolution scheme;
a credit provider or credit reporting body is a member of or subject to the scheme; or
the disclosure is required or authorised by or under an Australian law (other than the consumer data rules) or a court/tribunal order; or
the disclosure is a disclosure prescribed by the regulations.
Note: See section 21NA for additional rules about the disclosure of credit eligibility information under paragraph (3)(b) or (c).

However, if the credit eligibility information about the individual is, or was derived from, repayment history information or financial hardship information about the individual, the credit provider must not disclose the information under subsection (3).
Civil penalty: 2,000 penalty units.
Subsection (4) does not apply if:
the recipient of the credit eligibility information is another credit provider who is a licensee; or
the disclosure is a permitted CP disclosure within the meaning of section 21L; or
the credit provider discloses the credit eligibility information under paragraph (3)(b), (c), (e) or (f); or
the credit provider discloses the credit eligibility information under paragraph (3)(d) to an enforcement body.
Written note of use or disclosure
If a credit provider uses or discloses credit eligibility information under this section, the provider must make a written note of that use or disclosure.
Civil penalty: 500 penalty units.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If a credit provider is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principles 6, 7 and 8 do not apply to the provider in relation to credit eligibility information.
If:
a credit provider is an APP entity; and
the credit eligibility information is a government related identifier of the individual;
Australian Privacy Principle 9.2 does not apply to the provider in relation to the information.

section.heading: Permitted CP uses in relation to individuals

content.p: A use by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP use in relation to the individual if:
the relevant credit reporting information was disclosed to the provider under a provision specified in column 1 of the table for the purpose (if any) specified in that column; and
the provider uses the credit eligibility information for the purpose specified in column 2 of the table.

tr.td: The relevant credit reporting information was disclosed to the credit provider under ...
The credit provider uses the credit eligibility information for ...
item 1 of the table in subsection 20F(1) for the purpose of assessing an application for consumer credit made by the individual to the provider.

(a) a securitisation related purpose of the provider in relation to the individual; or (b) the internal management purposes of the provider that are directly related to the provision or management of consumer credit by the provider.
item 2 of the table in subsection 20F(1) for a particular commercial credit related purpose of the provider in relation to the individual.
that particular commercial credit related purpose.
item 2 of the table in subsection 20F(1) for the purpose of assessing an application for commercial credit made by a person to the provider.
the internal management purposes of the provider that are directly related to the provision or management of commercial credit by the provider.
item 3 of the table in subsection 20F(1) for a credit guarantee purpose of the provider in relation to the individual.
(a) the credit guarantee purpose; or (b) the internal management purposes of the provider that are directly related to the provision or management of any credit by the provider.
item 5 of the table in subsection 20F(1).
the purpose of assisting the individual to avoid defaulting on his or her obligations in relation to consumer credit provided by the provider to the individual.
item 6 of the table in subsection 20F(1) for a particular securitisation related purpose of the provider in relation to the individual.

section.heading: Permitted CP disclosures between credit providers

content.p: Consent
(1) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
(a) the disclosure is to another credit provider (the recipient) for a particular purpose; and
the recipient has an Australian link; and
the individual expressly consents to the disclosure of the information to the recipient for that purpose.
The consent of the individual under paragraph (1)(c):
must be given in writing unless:
the disclosure of the information to the recipient is for the purpose of assessing an application for consumer credit or commercial credit made to the recipient; and
the application has not been made in writing; and
must be given to the credit provider or recipient.
Agents of credit providers
(3) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
the provider is acting as an agent of another credit provider that has an Australian link; and
while the provider is so acting, the provider is a credit provider under subsection 6H(1); and
the provider discloses the information to the other credit provider in the provider’s capacity as such an agent.
Securitisation arrangements etc.
(4) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
the provider is a credit provider under subsection 6J(1) in relation to credit; and
(b) the credit has been provided by, or is credit for which an application has been made to, another credit provider (the original credit provider) that has an Australian link; and
the original credit provider is not a credit provider under that subsection; and
the information is disclosed to:
the original credit provider; or
another credit provider that is a credit provider under that subsection in relation to the credit and that has an Australian link; and
the disclosure of the information is reasonably necessary for:
purchasing, funding or managing, or processing an application for, the credit by means of a securitisation arrangement; or
undertaking credit enhancement in relation to the credit.
Mortgage credit secured by the same real property
(5) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
the disclosure is to another credit provider that has an Australian link; and
both credit providers have provided mortgage credit to the individual in relation to which the same real property forms all or part of the security; and
the individual is at least 60 days overdue in making a payment in relation to the mortgage credit provided by either provider; and
the information is disclosed for the purpose of either provider deciding what action to take in relation to the overdue payment.

section.heading: Permitted CP disclosures relating to guarantees etc.

content.p: Offer to act as a guarantor etc.
(1) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
either:
the provider has provided credit to the individual; or
the individual has applied to the provider for credit; and
the disclosure is to a person for the purpose of that person considering whether:
to offer to act as a guarantor in relation to the credit; or
to offer property as security for the credit; and
the person has an Australian link; and
the individual expressly consents to the disclosure of the information to the person for that purpose.
The consent of the individual under paragraph (1)(d) must be given in writing unless:
if subparagraph (1)(a)(i) applies—the application for the credit was not made in writing; or
if subparagraph (1)(a)(ii) applies—the application for the credit has not been made in writing.
Guarantors etc.
(3) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
the disclosure is to a person who:
is a guarantor in relation to credit provided by the provider to the individual; or
has provided property as security for such credit; and
the person has an Australian link; and
either:
the individual expressly consents to the disclosure of the information to the person; or
if subparagraph (a)(i) applies—the information is disclosed to the person for a purpose related to the enforcement, or proposed enforcement, of the guarantee.
The consent of the individual under subparagraph (3)(c)(i) must be given in writing unless the application for the credit was not made in writing.

section.heading: Permitted CP disclosures to mortgage insurers

content.p: A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if the disclosure is to a mortgage insurer that has an Australian link for:
a mortgage insurance purpose of the insurer in relation to the individual; or
any purpose arising under a contract for mortgage insurance that has been entered into between the provider and the insurer.

section.heading: Permitted CP disclosures to debt collectors

content.p: (1) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
the disclosure is to a person or body that carries on a business or undertaking that involves the collection of debts on behalf of others; and
the information is disclosed to the person or body for the primary purpose of the person or body collecting payments that are overdue in relation to:
consumer credit provided by the provider to the individual; or
commercial credit provided by the provider to a person; and
the information is information of a kind referred to in subsection (2).
Note: See section 21NA for additional rules about the disclosure of credit eligibility information under this subsection.
The information for the purposes of paragraph (1)(d) is:
identification information about the individual; or
court proceedings information about the individual; or
personal insolvency information about the individual; or
if subparagraph (1)(c)(i) applies—default information about the individual if:
the information relates to a payment that the individual is overdue in making in relation to consumer credit that has been provided by the credit provider to the individual; and
the provider does not hold, or has not held, payment information about the individual that relates to that overdue payment.

section.heading: Permitted CP disclosures to other recipients

content.p: Mortgage credit assistance schemes
(1) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
the disclosure is to a State or Territory authority; and
the functions or responsibilities of the authority include:
giving assistance (directly or indirectly) that facilitates the provision of mortgage credit to individuals; or
the management or supervision of schemes or arrangements under which such assistance is given; and
the information is disclosed for the purpose of enabling the authority:
to determine the extent of the assistance (if any) to give in relation to the provision of mortgage credit to the individual; or
to manage or supervise such a scheme or arrangement.
Assignment of debts owed to credit providers etc.
(2) A disclosure by a credit provider of credit eligibility information about an individual is a permitted CP disclosure in relation to the individual if:
(a) the disclosure is to one or more of the following (the recipient):
an entity;
a professional legal adviser of the entity;
a professional financial adviser of the entity; and
the recipient has an Australian link; and
subsection (3) applies to the information.
This subsection applies to the credit eligibility information if the recipient proposes to use the information:
in the process of the entity considering whether to:
accept an assignment of a debt owed to the credit provider; or
accept a debt owed to the provider as security for credit provided to the provider; or
purchase an interest in the provider or a related body corporate of the provider; or
in connection with exercising rights arising from the acceptance of such an assignment or debt, or the purchase of such an interest.

section.heading: Disclosures to certain persons and bodies that do not have an Australian link

content.p: Related bodies corporate and credit managers etc.

(1) Before a credit provider discloses credit eligibility information under paragraph 21G(3)(b) or (c) to a related body corporate, or person, that does not have an Australian link, the provider must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the body or person does not breach the following provisions (the relevant provisions) in relation to the information:
for a disclosure under paragraph 21G(3)(b)—section 22D;
for a disclosure under paragraph 21G(3)(c)—section 22E;
in both cases—the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principles 1, 6, 7, 8 and 9.2).
If:
a credit provider discloses credit eligibility information under paragraph 21G(3)(b) or (c) to a related body corporate, or person, that does not have an Australian link; and
the relevant provisions do not apply, under this Act, to an act done, or a practice engaged in, by the body or person in relation to the information; and
the body or person does an act, or engages in a practice, in relation to the information that would be a breach of the relevant provisions if those provisions applied to the act or practice;

the act done, or the practice engaged in, by the body or person is taken, for the purposes of this Act, to have been done, or engaged in, by the provider and to be a breach of those provisions by the provider.
Debt collectors

Before a credit provider discloses credit eligibility information under subsection 21M(1) to a person or body that does not have an Australian link, the provider must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the person or body does not breach the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principle 1) in relation to the information.
If:
a credit provider discloses credit eligibility information under subsection 21M(1) to a person or body that does not have an Australian link; and
the Australian Privacy Principles do not apply, under this Act, to an act done, or a practice engaged in, by the person or body in relation to the information; and

the person or body does an act, or engages in a practice, in relation to the information that would be a breach of the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principle 1) if those Australian Privacy Principles applied to the act or practice;

the act done, or the practice engaged in, by the person or body is taken, for the purposes of this Act, to have been done, or engaged in, by the provider and to be a breach of those Australian Privacy Principles by the provider.

section.heading: Notification of a refusal of an application for consumer credit

content.p: This section applies if:
a credit provider refuses an application for consumer credit made in Australia:
by an individual; or
(ii) jointly by an individual and one or more other persons (the other applicants); and
the refusal is based wholly or partly on credit eligibility information about one or more of the following:
the individual;
a person who is proposing to act as a guarantor in relation to the consumer credit;
if the application is an application of a kind referred to in subparagraph (a)(ii)—one of the other applicants; and
a credit reporting body disclosed the relevant credit reporting information to the provider for the purposes of assessing the application.
The credit provider must, within a reasonable period after refusing the application, give the individual a written notice that:
states that the application has been refused; and
states that the refusal is based wholly or partly on credit eligibility information about one or more of the persons referred to in paragraph (1)(b); and
if that information is about the individual—sets out:
the name and contact details of the credit reporting body that disclosed the relevant credit reporting information to the provider; and
any other matter specified in the registered CR code.
Subdivision E—Integrity of credit information and credit eligibility information

section.heading: Quality of credit eligibility information

content.p: A credit provider must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the credit eligibility information the provider collects is accurate, up-to-date and complete.

A credit provider must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the credit eligibility information the provider uses or discloses is, having regard to the purpose of the use or disclosure, accurate, up-to-date, complete and relevant.
If a credit provider is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principle 10 does not apply to the provider in relation to credit eligibility information.

section.heading: False or misleading credit information or credit eligibility information

content.p: Offences
A credit provider commits an offence if:
the provider discloses credit information under section 21D; and
the information is false or misleading in a material particular.
Penalty: 200 penalty units.
A credit provider commits an offence if:
the provider uses or discloses credit eligibility information under this Division; and
the information is false or misleading in a material particular.
Penalty: 200 penalty units.
Civil penalties
A credit provider must not disclose credit information under section 21D if the information is false or misleading in a material particular.
Civil penalty: 2,000 penalty units.
A credit provider must not use or disclose credit eligibility information under this Division if the information is false or misleading in a material particular.
Civil penalty: 2,000 penalty units.

section.heading: Security of credit eligibility information

content.p: If a credit provider holds credit eligibility information, the provider must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to protect the information:
from misuse, interference and loss; and
from unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.
If:
a credit provider holds credit eligibility information about an individual; and
the provider no longer needs the information for any purpose for which the information may be used or disclosed by the provider under this Division; and
the provider is not required by or under an Australian law, or a court/tribunal order, to retain the information;
the provider must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to destroy the information or to ensure that the information is de-identified.
Civil penalty: 1,000 penalty units.
If a credit provider is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principle 11 does not apply to the provider in relation to credit eligibility information.
Subdivision F—Access to, and correction of, information

section.heading: Access to credit eligibility information

content.p: Access

If a credit provider holds credit eligibility information about an individual, the provider must, on request by an access seeker in relation to the information, give the access seeker access to the information.
Exceptions to access
Despite subsection (1), the credit provider is not required to give the access seeker access to the credit eligibility information to the extent that:
giving access would be unlawful; or
denying access is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order; or
giving access would be likely to prejudice one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, an enforcement body.
Dealing with requests for access
The credit provider must respond to the request within a reasonable period after the request is made.
Means of access
If the credit provider gives access to the credit eligibility information, the access must be given in the manner set out in the registered CR code.
Access charges
If the credit provider is an agency, the provider must not charge the access seeker for the making of the request or for giving access to the information.

If a credit provider is an organisation or small business operator, any charge by the provider for giving access to the information must not be excessive and must not apply to the making of the request.
Refusal to give access
If the provider refuses to give access to the information because of subsection (2), the provider must give the access seeker a written notice that:
sets out the reasons for the refusal except to the extent that, having regard to the grounds for the refusal, it would be unreasonable to do so; and
states that, if the access seeker is not satisfied with the response to the request, the access seeker may:
access a recognised external dispute resolution scheme of which the provider is a member or to which it is subject; or
make a complaint to the Commissioner under Part V.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If a credit provider is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principle 12 does not apply to the provider in relation to credit eligibility information.

section.heading: Correction of credit information or credit eligibility information

content.p: If:
a credit provider holds credit information or credit eligibility information about an individual; and
the provider is satisfied that, having regard to a purpose for which the information is held by the provider, the information is inaccurate, out-of-date, incomplete, irrelevant or misleading;

the provider must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to correct the information to ensure that, having regard to the purpose for which it is held, the information is accurate, up-to-date, complete, relevant and not misleading.
Notice of correction
If:
the credit provider corrects credit information or credit eligibility information under subsection (1); and
the provider has previously disclosed the information under:
this Division (other than subsection 21V(4)); or
the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principle 4.2);
the provider must, within a reasonable period, give each recipient of the information written notice of the correction.
Subsection (2) does not apply if:
it is impracticable for the credit provider to give the notice under that subsection; or
the credit provider is required by or under an Australian law, or a court/tribunal order, not to give the notice under that subsection.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If a credit provider is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principle 13:
applies to the provider in relation to credit information or credit eligibility information that is identification information; but
does not apply to the provider in relation to any other kind of credit information or credit eligibility information.
Note: Identification information may be corrected under this section or Australian Privacy Principle 13.
Exemption for certain non-participating credit providers
This section does not apply to a non-participating credit provider.

section.heading: Individual may request the correction of credit information etc.

content.p: Request
An individual may request a credit provider to correct personal information about the individual if:
the personal information is:
credit information about the individual; or
CRB derived information about the individual; or
CP derived information about the individual; and
the provider holds at least one kind of the personal information referred to in paragraph (a).
Correction

If the credit provider is satisfied that the personal information is inaccurate, out-of-date, incomplete, irrelevant or misleading, the provider must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to correct the information within:
the period of 30 days that starts on the day on which the request is made; or
such longer period as the individual has agreed to in writing.
Consultation

(3) If the credit provider considers that the provider cannot be satisfied of the matter referred to in subsection (2) in relation to the personal information without consulting either or both of the following (the interested party):
a credit reporting body that holds or held the information and that has an Australian link;
another credit provider that holds or held the information and that has an Australian link;
the provider must consult that interested party, or those interested parties, about the individual’s request.

The use or disclosure of personal information about the individual for the purposes of the consultation is taken, for the purposes of this Act, to be a use or disclosure that is authorised by this subsection.
No charge
The credit provider must not charge the individual for the making of the request or for correcting the information.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If a credit provider is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principle 13:
applies to the provider in relation to personal information referred to in paragraph (1)(a) that is identification information; but
does not apply to the provider in relation to any other kind of personal information referred to in that paragraph.
Note: Identification information may be corrected under this section or Australian Privacy Principle 13.
Exemption for certain non-participating credit providers
This section does not apply to a non-participating credit provider.

section.heading: Notice of correction etc. must be given

content.p: This section applies if an individual requests a credit provider to correct personal information under subsection 21V(1).
Notice of correction etc.
If the credit provider corrects personal information about the individual under subsection 21V(2), the provider must, within a reasonable period:
give the individual written notice of the correction; and
if the provider consulted an interested party under subsection 21V(3) about the individual’s request—give the party written notice of the correction; and
if the correction relates to information that the provider has previously disclosed under:
this Division (other than subsection 21V(4)); or
the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principle 4.2);
give each recipient of the information written notice of the correction.
If the credit provider does not correct the personal information under subsection 21V(2), the provider must, within a reasonable period, give the individual written notice that:
states that the correction has not been made; and
sets out the provider’s reasons for not correcting the information (including evidence substantiating the correctness of the information); and
states that, if the individual is not satisfied with the response to the request, the individual may:
access a recognised external dispute resolution scheme of which the provider is a member or to which it is subject; or
make a complaint to the Commissioner under Part V.
Exceptions
Paragraph (2)(c) does not apply if it is impracticable for the credit provider to give the notice under that paragraph.
Subsection (2) or (3) does not apply if the credit provider is required by or under an Australian law, or a court/tribunal order, not to give the notice under that subsection.

section.heading: Guide to this Division

content.p: This Division sets out rules that apply to affected information recipients in relation to their handling of their regulated information.

If an affected information recipient is an APP entity, the rules apply in relation to the regulated information of the recipient in addition to, or instead of, any relevant Australian Privacy Principles.
Subdivision A—Consideration of information privacy

section.heading: Open and transparent management of regulated information

content.p: The object of this section is to ensure that an affected information recipient manages the regulated information of the recipient in an open and transparent way.
Compliance with this Division etc.
An affected information recipient must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to implement practices, procedures and systems relating to the recipient’s functions or activities that:
will ensure that the recipient complies with this Division and the registered CR code if it binds the recipient; and
will enable the recipient to deal with inquiries or complaints from individuals about the recipient’s compliance with this Division or the registered CR code if it binds the recipient.
Policy about the management of regulated information
An affected information recipient must have a clearly expressed and up-to-date policy about the recipient’s management of the regulated information of the recipient.
Without limiting subsection (3), the policy of the affected information recipient must contain the following information:
the kinds of regulated information that the recipient collects and holds, and how the recipient collects and holds that information;
the purposes for which the recipient collects, holds, uses and discloses regulated information;
how an individual may access regulated information about the individual that is held by the recipient and seek the correction of such information;
how an individual may complain about a failure of the recipient to comply with this Division or the registered CR code if it binds the recipient;
how the recipient will deal with such a complaint.
Availability of policy etc.
An affected information recipient must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to make the policy available:
free of charge; and
in such form as is appropriate.
Note: An affected information recipient will usually make the policy available on the recipient’s website.

If a person or body requests a copy, in a particular form, of the policy of an affected information recipient, the recipient must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to give the person or body a copy in that form.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If an affected information recipient is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principles 1.3 and 1.4 do not apply to the recipient in relation to the regulated information of the recipient.
Subdivision B—Dealing with regulated information

section.heading: Additional notification requirements for affected information recipients

content.p: If an affected information recipient is an APP entity, then the matters for the purposes of Australian Privacy Principle 5.1 include the following matters to the extent that the personal information referred to in that principle is regulated information of the recipient:

(a) that the policy (the credit reporting policy) of the recipient that is referred to in subsection 22A(3) contains information about how an individual may access the regulated information about the individual that is held by the recipient, and seek the correction of such information;

that the credit reporting policy of the recipient contains information about how an individual may complain about a failure of the recipient to comply with this Division or the registered CR code if it binds the recipient; and
that the credit reporting policy of the recipient contains information about how the recipient will deal with such a complaint.

section.heading: Use or disclosure of information by mortgage insurers or trade insurers

content.p: Prohibition on use or disclosure
If:
a mortgage insurer or trade insurer holds or held personal information about an individual; and
the information was disclosed to the insurer by a credit reporting body or credit provider under Division 2 or 3 of this Part;
the insurer must not use or disclose the information, or any personal information about the individual derived from that information.
Permitted uses
Civil penalty: 2,000 penalty units.
Subsection (1) does not apply to the use of the information if:
for a mortgage insurer—the use is for:
a mortgage insurance purpose of the insurer in relation to the individual; or
any purpose arising under a contract for mortgage insurance that has been entered into between the credit provider and the insurer; or
for a trade insurer—the use is for a trade insurance purpose of the insurer in relation to the individual; or
the use is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order.
Permitted disclosure
Subsection (1) does not apply to the disclosure of the information if the disclosure is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If the mortgage insurer or trade insurer is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principles 6, 7 and 8 do not apply to the insurer in relation to the information.
If:
the mortgage insurer or trade insurer is an APP entity; and
the information is a government related identifier of the individual;
Australian Privacy Principle 9.2 does not apply to the insurer in relation to the information.

section.heading: Use or disclosure of information by a related body corporate

content.p: Prohibition on use or disclosure
If:
a body corporate holds or held credit eligibility information about an individual; and
the information was disclosed to the body by a credit provider under paragraph 21G(3)(b);
the body must not use or disclose the information, or any personal information about the individual derived from that information.
Permitted use or disclosure
Civil penalty: 1,000 penalty units.

Subsection (1) does not apply to the use or disclosure of the information by the body corporate if the body would be permitted to use or disclose the information under section 21G if the body were the credit provider.
In determining whether the body corporate would be permitted to use or disclose the information under section 21G, assume that the body is whichever of the following is applicable:
the credit provider that has provided the relevant credit to the individual;
the credit provider to which the relevant application for credit was made by the individual.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If the body corporate is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principles 6, 7 and 8 do not apply to the body in relation to the information.
If:
the body corporate is an APP entity; and
the information is a government related identifier of the individual;
Australian Privacy Principle 9.2 does not apply to the body in relation to the information.

section.heading: Use or disclosure of information by credit managers etc.

content.p: Prohibition on use or disclosure
If:
a person holds or held credit eligibility information about an individual; and
the information was disclosed to the person by a credit provider under paragraph 21G(3)(c);
the person must not use or disclose the information, or any personal information about the individual derived from that information.
Permitted uses
Civil penalty: 1,000 penalty units.
Subsection (1) does not apply to the use of the information if:
the person uses the information for the purpose for which it was disclosed to the person under paragraph 21G(3)(c); or
the use is required or authorised by or under an Australian law (other than the consumer data rules) or a court/tribunal order.
Permitted disclosure
Subsection (1) does not apply to the disclosure of the information if:
the disclosure is to the credit provider; or
the disclosure is required or authorised by or under an Australian law (other than the consumer data rules) or a court/tribunal order.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If the person is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principles 6, 7 and 8 do not apply to the person in relation to the information.
If:
the person is an APP entity; and
the information is a government related identifier of the individual;
Australian Privacy Principle 9.2 does not apply to the person in relation to the information.

section.heading: Use or disclosure of information by advisers etc.

content.p: Prohibition on use or disclosure
If:
(a) any of the following (the recipient) holds or held credit eligibility information about an individual:
an entity;
a professional legal adviser of the entity;
a professional financial adviser of the entity; and
the information was disclosed to the recipient by a credit provider under subsection 21N(2);
the recipient must not use or disclose the information, or any personal information about the individual derived from that information.
Permitted uses
Civil penalty: 1,000 penalty units.
Subsection (1) does not apply to the use of the information if:
for a recipient that is the entity—the information is used for a matter referred to in subsection 21N(3); or
for a recipient that is the professional legal adviser, or professional financial adviser, of the entity—the information is used:
in the adviser’s capacity as an adviser of the entity; and
in connection with advising the entity about a matter referred to in subsection 21N(3); or
the use is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order.
Permitted disclosure
Subsection (1) does not apply to the disclosure of the information if the disclosure is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order.
Interaction with the Australian Privacy Principles
If the recipient is an APP entity, Australian Privacy Principles 6, 7 and 8 do not apply to the recipient in relation to the information.
If:
the recipient is an APP entity; and
the information is a government related identifier of the individual;
Australian Privacy Principle 9.2 does not apply to the recipient in relation to the information.

section.heading: Guide to this Division

content.p: This Division deals with complaints about credit reporting bodies or credit providers.
Individuals may complain to credit reporting bodies or credit providers about acts or practices that may be a breach of certain provisions of this Part or the registered CR code.
If a complaint is made, the respondent for the complaint must investigate the complaint and make a decision about the complaint.

section.heading: Individual may complain about a breach of a provision of this Part etc.

content.p: Complaint
An individual may complain to a credit reporting body about an act or practice engaged in by the body that may be a breach of either of the following provisions in relation to the individual:
a provision of this Part (other than section 20R or 20T);
a provision of the registered CR code (other than a provision that relates to that section).
Note: A complaint about a breach of section 20R or 20T, or a provision of the registered CR code that relates to that section, may be made to the Commissioner under Part V.
An individual may complain to a credit provider about an act or practice engaged in by the provider that may be a breach of either of the following provisions in relation to the individual:
a provision of this Part (other than section 21T or 21V);
a provision of the registered CR code (other than a provision that relates to that section) if it binds the credit provider.
Note: A complaint about a breach of section 21T or 21V, or a provision of the registered CR code that relates to that section, may be made to the Commissioner under Part V.
Nature of complaint
If an individual makes a complaint, the individual must specify the nature of the complaint.
The complaint may relate to personal information that has been destroyed or de-identified.
No charge
The credit reporting body or credit provider must not charge the individual for the making of the complaint or for dealing with the complaint.

section.heading: Dealing with complaints

content.p: If an individual makes a complaint under section 23A, the respondent for the complaint:
must, within 7 days after the complaint is made, give the individual a written notice that:
acknowledges the making of the complaint; and
sets out how the respondent will deal with the complaint; and
must investigate the complaint.
Consultation about the complaint
If the respondent for the complaint considers that it is necessary to consult a credit reporting body or credit provider about the complaint, the respondent must consult the body or provider.

The use or disclosure of personal information about the individual for the purposes of the consultation is taken, for the purposes of this Act, to be a use or disclosure that is authorised by this subsection.
Decision about the complaint
After investigating the complaint, the respondent must, within the period referred to in subsection (5), make a decision about the complaint and give the individual a written notice that:
sets out the decision; and
states that, if the individual is not satisfied with the decision, the individual may:
access a recognised external dispute resolution scheme of which the respondent is a member or to which it is subject; or
make a complaint to the Commissioner under Part V.
The period for the purposes of subsection (4) is:
the period of 30 days that starts on the day on which the complaint is made; or
such longer period as the individual has agreed to in writing.

section.heading: Notification requirements relating to correction complaints

content.p: This section applies if an individual makes a complaint under section 23A about an act or practice that may breach section 20S or 21U (which deal with the correction of personal information by credit reporting bodies and credit providers).
Notification of complaint etc.
If:
the respondent for the complaint is a credit reporting body; and
the complaint relates to credit information or credit eligibility information that a credit provider holds;
the respondent must, in writing:
notify the provider of the making of the complaint as soon as practicable after it is made; and
notify the provider of the making of a decision about the complaint under subsection 23B(4) as soon as practicable after it is made.
If:
the respondent for the complaint is a credit provider; and
the complaint relates to:
credit reporting information that a credit reporting body holds; or
credit information or credit eligibility information that another credit provider holds;
the respondent must, in writing:
notify the body or other provider (as the case may be) of the making of the complaint as soon as practicable after it is made; and
notify the body or other provider (as the case may be) of the making of a decision about the complaint under subsection 23B(4) as soon as practicable after it is made.
Notification of recipients of disclosed information
If:
a credit reporting body discloses credit reporting information to which the complaint relates under Division 2 of this Part; and
at the time of the disclosure, a decision about the complaint under subsection 23B(4) has not been made;
the body must, at that time, notify in writing the recipient of the information of the complaint.
If:
a credit provider discloses personal information to which the complaint relates under Division 3 of this Part or under the Australian Privacy Principles; and
at the time of the disclosure, a decision about the complaint under subsection 23B(4) has not been made;
the provider must, at that time, notify in writing the recipient of the information of the complaint.
Exceptions
Subsection (2), (3), (4) or (5) does not apply if:
it is impracticable for the credit reporting body or credit provider to give the notification under that subsection; or
the credit reporting body or credit provider is required by or under an Australian law, or a court/tribunal order, not to give the notification under that subsection.

division.heading: Unauthorised obtaining of credit reporting information etc.

section.heading: Obtaining credit reporting information from a credit reporting body

content.p: Offences
An entity commits an offence if:
the entity obtains credit reporting information; and
the information is obtained from a credit reporting body; and
the entity is not:
an entity to which the body is permitted to disclose the information under Division 2 of this Part; or
an access seeker for the information.
Penalty: 200 penalty units.
An entity commits an offence if:
the entity obtains credit reporting information; and
the information is obtained from a credit reporting body; and
the information is obtained by false pretence.
Penalty: 200 penalty units.
Civil penalties
An entity must not obtain credit reporting information from a credit reporting body if the entity is not:
an entity to which the body is permitted to disclose the information under Division 2 of this Part; or
an access seeker for the information.
Civil penalty: 2,000 penalty units.
An entity must not obtain, by false pretence, credit reporting information from a credit reporting body.
Civil penalty: 2,000 penalty units.

section.heading: Obtaining credit eligibility information from a credit provider

content.p: Offences
An entity commits an offence if:
the entity obtains credit eligibility information; and
the information is obtained from a credit provider; and
the entity is not:
an entity to which the provider is permitted to disclose the information under Division 3 of this Part; or
an access seeker for the information.
Penalty: 200 penalty units.
An entity commits an offence if:
the entity obtains credit eligibility information; and
the information is obtained from a credit provider; and
the information is obtained by false pretence.
Penalty: 200 penalty units.
Civil penalties
An entity must not obtain credit eligibility information from a credit provider if the entity is not:
an entity to which the provider is permitted to disclose the information under Division 3 of this Part; or
an access seeker for the information.
Civil penalty: 2,000 penalty units.
An entity must not obtain, by false pretence, credit eligibility information from a credit provider.
Civil penalty: 2,000 penalty units.

section.heading: Compensation orders

content.p: The Federal Court or the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) may order an entity to compensate a person for loss or damage (including injury to the person’s feelings or humiliation) suffered by the person if:
either:
a civil penalty order has been made under subsection 82(3) of the Regulatory Powers Act against the entity for a contravention of a civil penalty provision of this Part; or
the entity is found guilty of an offence against this Part; and
that loss or damage resulted from the contravention or commission of the offence.
The order must specify the amount of compensation.
The court may make the order only if:
the person applies for an order under this section; and
the application is made within 6 years of the day the cause of action that relates to the contravention or commission of the offence accrued.
If the court makes the order, the amount of compensation specified in the order that is to be paid to the person may be recovered as a debt due to the person.

section.heading: Other orders to compensate loss or damage

content.p: This section applies if:
either:
a civil penalty order has been made under subsection 82(3) of the Regulatory Powers Act against the entity for a contravention of a civil penalty provision of this Part; or
an entity is found guilty of an offence against this Part; and
a person has suffered, or is likely to suffer, loss or damage (including injury to the person’s feelings or humiliation) as a result of the contravention or commission of the offence.
The Federal Court or the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2) may make such order as the Court considers appropriate against the entity to:
compensate the person, in whole or in part, for that loss or damage; or
prevent or reduce that loss or damage suffered, or likely to be suffered, by the person.
Without limiting subsection (2), examples of orders the court may make include:
an order directing the entity to perform any reasonable act, or carry out any reasonable course of conduct, to redress the loss or damage suffered by the person; and

an order directing the entity to pay the person a specified amount to reimburse the person for expenses reasonably incurred by the person in connection with the contravention or commission of the offence; and
an order directing the defendant to pay to the person the amount of loss or damage the plaintiff suffered.
The court may make the order only if:
the person applies for an order under this section; and
the application is made within 6 years of the day the cause of action that relates to the contravention or commission of the offence accrued.
If the court makes an order that the entity pay an amount to the person, the person may recover the amount as a debt due to the person.

section.heading: Review of operation of this Part

content.p: The Minister must cause an independent review to be conducted of the operation of this Part.
The persons who conduct the review must complete it, and give the Minister a written report of the review, before 1 October 2024.
The Minister must cause a copy of the report to be tabled in each House of the Parliament within 15 sitting days of that House after the report is given to the Minister.

section.heading: Guide to this Part

content.p: This Part deals with privacy codes.
Division 2 deals with codes of practice about information privacy, called APP codes. APP code developers or the Commissioner may develop APP codes, which:
must set out how one or more of the Australian Privacy Principles are to be applied or complied with; and
may impose additional requirements to those imposed by the Australian Privacy Principles; and
may deal with other specified matters.

If the Commissioner includes an APP code on the Codes Register, an APP entity bound by the code must not breach it. A breach of a registered APP code is an interference with the privacy of an individual.
Division 3 deals with a code of practice about credit reporting, called a CR code. CR code developers or the Commissioner may develop a CR code, which:
must set out how one or more of the provisions of Part IIIA are to be applied or complied with; and
must deal with matters required or permitted by Part IIIA to be provided for by the registered CR code; and
may deal with other specified matters.
If the Commissioner includes a CR code on the Codes Register, an entity bound by the code must not breach it. A breach of the registered CR code is an interference with the privacy of an individual.
Division 4 deals with the Codes Register, guidelines relating to codes and the review of the operation of registered codes.
Subdivision A—Compliance with registered APP codes etc.

section.heading: APP entities to comply with binding registered APP codes

content.p: An APP entity must not do an act, or engage in a practice, that breaches a registered APP code that binds the entity.

section.heading: What is a registered APP code

content.p: (1) A registered APP code is an APP code:
that is included on the Codes Register; and
that is in force.
A registered APP code is a legislative instrument.
(3) Subsection 12(2) (retrospective application of legislative instruments) of the Legislation Act 2003 does not apply to a registered APP code.
Note: An APP code cannot come into force before it is included on the Codes Register: see paragraph 26C(2)(c).

section.heading: What is an APP code

content.p: (1) An APP code is a written code of practice about information privacy.
An APP code must:
set out how one or more of the Australian Privacy Principles are to be applied or complied with; and
specify the APP entities that are bound by the code, or a way of determining the APP entities that are bound by the code; and
set out the period during which the code is in force (which must not start before the day the code is registered under section 26H).
An APP code may do one or more of the following:

impose additional requirements to those imposed by one or more of the Australian Privacy Principles, so long as the additional requirements are not contrary to, or inconsistent with, those principles;
cover an act or practice that is exempt within the meaning of subsection 7B(1), (2) or (3);
deal with the internal handling of complaints;
provide for the reporting to the Commissioner about complaints;
deal with any other relevant matters.
An APP code may be expressed to apply to any one or more of the following:
all personal information or a specified type of personal information;
a specified activity, or a specified class of activities, of an APP entity;
a specified industry sector or profession, or a specified class of industry sectors or professions;
APP entities that use technology of a specified kind.
(4A) Without limiting subsection 33(3A) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901, an APP code may provide differently for different:
classes of entities; and
classes of personal information; and
classes of activities of entities.
An APP code is not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Extension of Act to exempt acts or practices covered by registered APP codes

content.p: If a registered APP code covers an act or practice that is exempt within the meaning of subsection 7B(1), (2) or (3), this Act applies in relation to the code as if that act or practice were not exempt.
Subdivision B—Development and registration of APP codes

section.heading: Development of APP codes by APP code developers

content.p: Own initiative
An APP code developer may develop an APP code.
At the Commissioner’s request

The Commissioner may, in writing, request an APP code developer to develop an APP code, and apply to the Commissioner for the code to be registered, if the Commissioner is satisfied it is in the public interest for the code to be developed.
The request must:
specify the period within which the request must be complied with; and
set out the effect of section 26A.
The period:
must run for at least 120 days from the date the request is made; and
may be extended by the Commissioner.
The request may:
specify one or more matters that the APP code must deal with; and
specify the APP entities, or a class of APP entities, that should be bound by the code.

Despite paragraph (5)(a), the Commissioner must not require an APP code to cover an act or practice that is exempt within the meaning of subsection 7B(1), (2) or (3). However, the APP code that is developed by the APP code developer may cover such an act or practice.
The Commissioner must make a copy of the request publicly available as soon as practicable after the request is made.

section.heading: Application for registration of APP codes

content.p: If an APP code developer develops an APP code, the developer may apply to the Commissioner for registration of the code.
Before making the application, the APP code developer must:
make a draft of the APP code publicly available; and
invite the public to make submissions to the developer about the draft within a specified period (which must run for at least 28 days); and
give consideration to any submissions made within the specified period.
The application must:
be made in the form and manner specified by the Commissioner; and
be accompanied by such information as is specified by the Commissioner.
The APP code developer may vary the APP code at any time before the Commissioner registers the code, but only with the consent of the Commissioner.

section.heading: Development of APP codes by the Commissioner—following a request

content.p: This section applies if the Commissioner made a request under subsection 26E(2) and either:
the request has not been complied with; or
the request has been complied with but the Commissioner has decided not to register, under section 26H, the APP code that was developed as requested.

The Commissioner may develop an APP code if the Commissioner is satisfied that it is in public interest to develop the code. However, despite subsection 26C(3)(b), the APP code must not cover an act or practice that is exempt within the meaning of subsection 7B(1), (2) or (3).
Before registering the APP code under section 26H, the Commissioner must:
make a draft of the code publicly available; and
invite the public to make submissions to the Commissioner about the draft within a specified period (which must run for at least 28 days); and
give consideration to any submissions made within the specified period.

section.heading: Development of APP codes by the Commissioner—at the direction of the Minister

content.p: Minister may give direction
(1) The Minister may, in writing, direct the Commissioner to develop an APP code if the Minister is satisfied that it is in the public interest:
to develop the code; and
for the Commissioner to develop the code.
Without limiting subsection (1), a direction under that subsection may:
specify one or more matters that the code must deal with; and
specify the APP entities, or a class of APP entities, that are to be bound by the code.
A direction under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.
Commissioner must develop and register code
The Commissioner must develop and register an APP code if the Minister has given the Commissioner a direction under subsection (1) to develop the code.
Matters covered by code
Despite paragraph 26C(3)(b), the APP code must not cover an act or practice that is exempt within the meaning of subsection 7B(1), (2) or (3).
Consultation etc.
In developing the APP code, the Commissioner may consult any person the Commissioner considers appropriate.
Before registering the APP code under section 26H, the Commissioner must:
make a draft of the code publicly available; and
invite the public to make submissions to the Commissioner about the draft within a specified period (which must run for at least 40 days); and
give consideration to any submissions made within the specified period.

section.heading: Development of APP codes by the Commissioner—temporary APP codes

content.p: Minister may give direction
(1) The Minister may, in writing, direct the Commissioner to develop an APP code (a temporary APP code) if the Minister is satisfied that:
it is in the public interest:
to develop the code; and
for the Commissioner to develop the code; and
the code should be developed urgently.
Without limiting subsection (1), a direction under that subsection may:
specify one or more matters that the code must deal with; and
specify the APP entities, or a class of APP entities, that should be bound by the code.
A direction under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.
Commissioner must develop and register code
The Commissioner must develop and register a temporary APP code if the Minister has given the Commissioner a direction under subsection (1) to develop the code.
Matters covered by code
However, despite paragraph 26C(3)(b), the temporary APP code must not cover an act or practice that is exempt within the meaning of subsection 7B(1), (2) or (3).
Consultation etc.
In developing the temporary APP code, the Commissioner may consult any person the Commissioner considers appropriate.
Period code is in force
The period set out for the temporary APP code for the purposes of paragraph 26C(2)(c) must not be longer than 12 months.
Note: Paragraph 26C(2)(c) deals with the period during which the code is in force.
Disallowance
(8) Section 42 (disallowance) of the Legislation Act 2003 does not apply to a temporary APP code that is a registered APP code.
Note: A registered APP code is a legislative instrument: see subsection 26B(2).

section.heading: Development of APP codes by the Commissioner—Children’s Online Privacy Code

content.p: Children’s Online Privacy Code
(1) The Commissioner must develop an APP code (the Children’s Online Privacy Code) about online privacy for children.
The other provisions of this Division (including section 26C) apply in relation to the Children’s Online Privacy Code subject to this section.
Note: Section 26C deals with requirements for APP codes generally.
Matters covered by code

For the purposes of paragraph 26C(2)(a), the Children’s Online Privacy Code must set out how one or more of the Australian Privacy Principles are to be applied or complied with in relation to the privacy of children.

For the purposes of subsections 26C(3) and (4), the Children’s Online Privacy Code may provide for one or more of the matters mentioned in those subsections in relation to the privacy of children. However, despite paragraph 26C(3)(b), the code must not cover an act or practice that is exempt within the meaning of subsection 7B(1), (2) or (3).
Note: Codes may provide differently for different things: see subsection 26C(4A).
Entities bound by code
Subject to subsection (7), an APP entity is bound by the Children’s Online Privacy Code if:
all of the following apply:
(i) the entity is a provider of a social media service, relevant electronic service or designated internet service (all within the meaning of the Online Safety Act 2021);
the service is likely to be accessed by children;
the entity is not providing a health service; or
the entity is an APP entity, or an APP entity in a class of entities, specified in the code for the purposes of this paragraph.
Note: In relation to subparagraph (a)(ii), see subsection (11).
Paragraph 26C(2)(b) does not apply in relation to the Children’s Online Privacy Code.
Specified entities not bound by code

Despite subsection (5), an APP entity is not bound by the Children’s Online Privacy Code if the entity is an APP entity, or an APP entity in a class of entities, specified in the code for the purposes of this subsection.
Requirements
In developing the Children’s Online Privacy Code, the Commissioner may:
consult with:
children; and
relevant organisations or bodies concerned with children’s welfare; and
industry organisations or bodies representing the interests of one or more entities that may potentially be bound by the Code;
the eSafety Commissioner; and
the National Children’s Commissioner; and
consult any other person the Commissioner considers appropriate.
Before registering the Children’s Online Privacy Code under section 26H, the Commissioner must:
make a draft of the code publicly available; and
invite the public to make submissions to the Commissioner about the draft within a specified period (which must run for at least 60 days); and
give consideration to any submissions made within the specified period; and
consult with:
the eSafety Commissioner; and
the National Children’s Commissioner.
Time by which code must be made

(10) The Commissioner must develop and register the Children’s Online Privacy Code within the period of 24 months beginning on the day the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 receives the Royal Assent.
Services likely to be accessed by children
The Commissioner may make written guidelines to assist entities to determine if a service is likely to be accessed by children for the purposes of subparagraph (5)(a)(ii).
The Commissioner may publish any such guidelines on the Commissioner’s website.
Guidelines under subsection (11) are not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Commissioner may register APP codes

content.p: If:
an application for registration of an APP code is made under section 26F; or
the Commissioner develops an APP code under section 26G, 26GA or 26GB; or
the Commissioner develops a Children’s Online Privacy Code under section 26GC;
the Commissioner may register the code by including it on the Codes Register.
In deciding whether to register the APP code, the Commissioner may:
consult any person the Commissioner considers appropriate; and
consider the matters specified in any relevant guidelines made under section 26V.

If the Commissioner decides not to register an APP code developed by an APP code developer, the Commissioner must give written notice of the decision to the developer, including reasons for the decision.
Subdivision C—Variation and removal of registered APP codes

section.heading: Variation of registered APP codes

content.p: The Commissioner may, in writing, approve a variation of a registered APP code:
on his or her own initiative; or
on application by an APP entity that is bound by the code; or
on application by a body or association representing one or more APP entities that are bound by the code.
An application under paragraph (1)(b) or (c) must:
be made in the form and manner specified by the Commissioner; and
be accompanied by such information as is specified by the Commissioner.

If the Commissioner varies a registered APP code on his or her own initiative, then, despite subsection 26C(3)(b), the variation must not deal with an act or practice that is exempt within the meaning of subsection 7B(1), (2) or (3).
Before deciding whether to approve a variation, the Commissioner must:
make a draft of the variation publicly available; and
consult any person the Commissioner considers appropriate about the variation; and
consider the extent to which members of the public have been given an opportunity to comment on the variation.
In deciding whether to approve a variation, the Commissioner may consider the matters specified in any relevant guidelines made under section 26V.
(6) If the Commissioner approves a variation of a registered APP code (the original code), the Commissioner must:
remove the original code from the Codes Register; and
register the APP code, as varied, by including it on the Register.

If the Commissioner approves a variation, the variation comes into effect on the day specified in the approval, which must not be before the day on which the APP code, as varied, is included on the Codes Register.
An approval is not a legislative instrument.
Note: The APP code, as varied, is a legislative instrument once it is included on the Codes Register: see section 26B.

section.heading: Removal of registered APP codes

content.p: The Commissioner may remove a registered APP code from the Codes Register:
on his or her own initiative; or
on application by an APP entity that is bound by the code; or
on application by a body or association representing one or more APP entities that are bound by the code.
An application under paragraph (1)(b) or (c) must:
be made in the form and manner specified by the Commissioner; and
be accompanied by such information as is specified by the Commissioner.
Before deciding whether to remove the registered APP code, the Commissioner must:
consult any person the Commissioner considers appropriate about the proposed removal; and
consider the extent to which members of the public have been given an opportunity to comment on the proposed removal.
In deciding whether to remove the registered APP code, the Commissioner may consider the matters specified in any relevant guidelines made under section 26V.
Subdivision A—Compliance with the registered CR code

section.heading: Entities to comply with the registered CR code if bound by the code

content.p: If an entity is bound by the registered CR code, the entity must not do an act, or engage in a practice, that breaches the code.
Note: There must always be one, and only one, registered CR code at all times after this Part commences: see subsection 26S(4).

section.heading: What is the registered CR code

content.p: (1) The registered CR code is the CR code that is included on the Codes Register.
The registered CR code is a legislative instrument.
(3) Subsection 12(2) (retrospective application of legislative instruments) of the Legislation Act 2003 does not apply to the registered CR code.

section.heading: What is a CR code

content.p: (1) A CR code is a written code of practice about credit reporting.
A CR code must:
set out how one or more of the provisions of Part IIIA are to be applied or complied with; and
make provision for, or in relation to, matters required or permitted by Part IIIA to be provided for by the registered CR code; and
bind all credit reporting bodies; and
specify the credit providers that are bound by the code, or a way of determining which credit providers are bound; and
specify any other entities subject to Part IIIA that are bound by the code, or a way of determining which of those entities are bound.
A CR code may do one or more of the following:
impose additional requirements to those imposed by Part IIIA, so long as the additional requirements are not contrary to, or inconsistent with, that Part;
deal with the internal handling of complaints;
provide for the reporting to the Commissioner about complaints;
deal with any other relevant matters.
A CR code may be expressed to apply differently in relation to:
classes of entities that are subject to Part IIIA; and
specified classes of credit information, credit reporting information or credit eligibility information; and
specified classes of activities of entities that are subject to Part IIIA.
A CR code is not a legislative instrument.
Subdivision B—Development and registration of CR code

section.heading: Development of CR code by CR code developers

content.p: The Commissioner may, in writing, request a CR code developer to develop a CR code and apply to the Commissioner for the code to be registered.
The request must:
specify the period within which the request must be complied with; and
set out the effect of section 26L.
The period:
must run for at least 120 days from the date the request is made; and
may be extended by the Commissioner.
The request may:
specify one or more matters that the CR code must deal with; and
specify the credit providers, or a class of credit providers, that should be bound by the code; and
specify the other entities, or a class of other entities, subject to Part IIIA that should be bound by the code.
The Commissioner must make a copy of the request publicly available as soon as practicable after the request is made.

section.heading: Application for registration of CR code

content.p: If a CR code developer develops a CR code, the developer may apply to the Commissioner for registration of the code.
Before making the application, the CR code developer must:
make a draft of the CR code publicly available; and
invite the public to make submissions to the developer about the draft within a specified period (which must run for at least 28 days); and
give consideration to any submissions made within the specified period.
The application must:
be made in the form and manner specified by the Commissioner; and
be accompanied by such information as is specified by the Commissioner.
The CR code developer may vary the CR code at any time before the Commissioner registers the code, but only with the consent of the Commissioner.

section.heading: Development of CR code by the Commissioner

content.p: The Commissioner may develop a CR code if the Commissioner made a request under section 26P and either:
the request has not been complied with; or
the request has been complied with but the Commissioner has decided not to register, under section 26S, the CR code that was developed as requested.
Before registering the CR code under section 26S, the Commissioner must:
make a draft of the code publicly available; and
invite the public to make submissions to the Commissioner about the draft within a specified period (which must run for at least 28 days); and
give consideration to any submissions made within the specified period.

section.heading: Commissioner may register CR code

content.p: If:
an application for registration of a CR code is made under section 26Q; or
the Commissioner develops a CR code under section 26R;
the Commissioner may register the code by including it on the Codes Register.
In deciding whether to register the CR code, the Commissioner may:
consult any person the Commissioner considers appropriate; and
consider the matters specified in any guidelines made under section 26V.
If the Commissioner decides not to register a CR code developed by a CR code developer, the Commissioner must give written notice of the decision to the developer, including reasons for the decision.
The Commissioner must ensure that there is one, and only one, registered CR code at all times after this Part commences.
Subdivision C—Variation of the registered CR code

section.heading: Variation of the registered CR code

content.p: The Commissioner may, in writing, approve a variation of the registered CR code:
on his or her own initiative; or
on application by an entity that is bound by the code; or
on application by a body or association representing one or more of the entities that are bound by the code.
An application under paragraph (1)(b) or (c) must:
be made in the form and manner specified by the Commissioner; and
be accompanied by such information as is specified by the Commissioner.
Before deciding whether to approve a variation, the Commissioner must:
make a draft of the variation publicly available; and
consult any person the Commissioner considers appropriate about the variation; and
consider the extent to which members of the public have been given an opportunity to comment on the variation.
In deciding whether to approve a variation, the Commissioner may consider the matters specified in any relevant guidelines made under section 26V.
(5) If the Commissioner approves a variation of the registered CR code (the original code), the Commissioner must:
remove the original code from the Codes Register; and
register the CR code, as varied, by including it on the Register.

If the Commissioner approves a variation, the variation comes into effect on the day specified in the approval, which must not be before the day on which the CR code, as varied, is included on the Codes Register.
An approval is not a legislative instrument.
Note: The CR code, as varied, is a legislative instrument once it is included on the Codes Register: see section 26M.

section.heading: Codes Register

content.p: (1) The Commissioner must keep a register (the Codes Register) which includes:
the APP codes the Commissioner has decided to register under section 26H; and
the APP codes the Commissioner must register under section 26J; and
the CR code the Commissioner has decided to register under section 26S; and
the CR code the Commissioner must register under section 26T.
Despite subsection (1), the Commissioner is not required to include on the Codes Register:
an APP code removed from the Register under section 26J or 26K; or
the CR code removed from the Register under section 26T.
The Commissioner must make the Codes Register available on the Commissioner’s website.
The Commissioner may charge fees for providing copies of, or extracts from, the Codes Register.

section.heading: Guidelines relating to codes

content.p: The Commissioner may make written guidelines:
to assist APP code developers to develop APP codes; or
to assist APP entities bound by registered APP codes to apply or comply with the codes; or
to assist CR code developers to develop a CR code; or
to assist entities bound by the registered CR code to apply or comply with the code.
The Commissioner may make written guidelines about matters the Commissioner may consider in deciding whether:
to register an APP code or a CR code; or
to approve a variation of a registered APP code or the registered CR code; or
to remove a registered APP code from the Codes Register.
The Commissioner may publish any such guidelines on the Commissioner’s website.
Guidelines are not a legislative instrument.

section.heading: Review of operation of registered codes

content.p: The Commissioner may review the operation of a registered APP code.
Note: The review may inform a decision by the Commissioner to approve a variation of a registered APP code or to remove a registered APP code from the Codes Register.
The Commissioner may review the operation of the registered CR code.
Note: The review may inform a decision by the Commissioner to approve a variation of the registered CR code.

section.heading: Guide to this Part

content.p: • This Part sets up a scheme for notification of eligible data breaches.
• An eligible data breach happens if:
there is unauthorised access to, unauthorised disclosure of, or loss of, personal information held by an entity; and
the access, disclosure or loss is likely to result in serious harm to any of the individuals to whom the information relates.
• An entity must give a notification if:
it has reasonable grounds to believe that an eligible data breach has happened; or
it is directed to do so by the Commissioner.
• The Commissioner may obtain information or documents in relation to actual or suspected eligible data breaches.
• This Part also deals with the collection, use and disclosure of personal information involved in eligible data breaches.

section.heading: Entity

content.p: For the purposes of this Part, entity includes a person who is a file number recipient.

section.heading: Deemed holding of information

content.p: Overseas recipients
If:
an APP entity has disclosed personal information about one or more individuals to an overseas recipient; and
Australian Privacy Principle 8.1 applied to the disclosure of the personal information; and
the overseas recipient holds the personal information;
this Part has effect as if:
the personal information were held by the APP entity; and
the APP entity were required under section 15 not to do an act, or engage in a practice, that breaches Australian Privacy Principle 11.1 in relation to the personal information.
Bodies or persons with no Australian link
If:
either:

a credit provider has disclosed, under paragraph 21G(3)(b) or (c), credit eligibility information about one or more individuals to a related body corporate, or person, that does not have an Australian link; or
a credit provider has disclosed, under subsection 21M(1), credit eligibility information about one or more individuals to a body or person that does not have an Australian link; and
the related body corporate, body or person holds the credit eligibility information;
this Part has effect as if:
the credit eligibility information were held by the credit provider; and
the credit provider were required to comply with subsection 21S(1) in relation to the credit eligibility information.
Note: See section 21NA.

section.heading: Exception—notification under the My Health Records Act 2012

content.p: If:
an unauthorised access to information; or
